newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: SE Asian Cocoa- Markets mixed as world prices jump.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Cocoa- Markets mixed as world prices jump.

text.p: The Southeast Asian cocoa market is expected to have a mixed week ahead, with buyers in Malaysia sidelined with comfortable stocks, while Indonesia looks for more supply as world prices rally, traders said on Wednesday.
Bean prices jumped in both countries on Wednesday in line with gains in New York where values touched their highest level in a month overnight, traders said.
However, demand in Malaysia remained soft, with grinders citing adequate supply from imports in recent months.
"I think we have covered out positions until July," Brendan Teh, marketing manager at Guan Chong Cocoa Manufacturers Sdn Bhd, said.
"The market has been quiet and hasn't seen much demand in the last few months, but there's been no shortage of supply," Teh said.
Malaysia producers said the market will see more beans from April, when the first harvest begins.
"The market is now being driven by production in the Ivory Coast and speculation in New York," he said.

On Wednesday, the Malaysian Cocoa Board quoted Standard Malaysian Cocoa Grade 1A out of Tawau, the country's main growing area, at an average of 3,040 ringgit a tonne. This compared with an average of 2,815 for SMC 1A a week ago.

In Indonesia, traders said the arrival of cocoa beans in Ujung Pandang, capital of the key producing area of South Sulawesi, was beginning to rise although the main crop harvest was still in the early stage, with the peak coming in May.

"Prices are getting better after the sharp increase in New York yesterday," one trader said. "I am looking to buy around 150 tonnes today, but there's a chance sellers might want to hold back as they anticipate prices to rise further."
Traders said the increase in local prices could see sellers wanting to get out of contracts they had done at lower prices.
"This happens when there's a sharp increase in prices," one trader said. "They try to delay delivery of cocoa bought at the lower levels, and try to open new contracts at higher prices."

The gains in New York were attributed to speculation that prices had touched bottom amid signs that consumption levels remain strong coupled with ongoing concerns that the hot weather in the Ivory Coast could harm the country's midcrop.
Indonesian cocoa was quoted at 2,660-2,750 rupiah a kg in Ujung Pandang, compared with 2,630-2,660 rupiah on Tuesday.
Indonesian traders said they expected New York to keep its momentum on Wednesday, with May futures opening $10 higher.
"I expect New York prices to open $10 higher today," a trader in Jakarta said. "I think the market has got some steam left."
